title: Is the problem real?
principle: A clumsy fix people already put up with proves the pain.

screens.text: Let me start in Bengaluru, around 2005. A young man named P.C. Musthafa often spent time at his cousin's grocery shop. The shop sold idli-dosa batter from a local maker, in a plain plastic bag tied with a rubber band. It had no brand and no maker's name.

screens.prompt: Buyers complained about that batter: the messy bags, the quality, the cleanliness. What do you think happened to its sales?

options.label: They fell. People stopped buying it
They stayed steady. People kept buying
Only a few loyal buyers stayed

screens.why: They stayed steady. One report puts it plainly: there were complaints, but sales didn't fall. People didn't like the bag, but they still wanted ready batter.

screens.title: The clue in the bag
screens.text: Musthafa saw a clue. People complained about the bags, but they kept paying for them. In 2006, he and four cousins started iD, their own batter brand, in a tiny room next to the shop. By 2015, iD sold about ₹100 crore a year.

screens.title: The workaround test
screens.text: A workaround is a clumsy fix people use because nothing better exists. A famous American school for new companies calls the worst pain a "hair on fire" problem: with your hair on fire, you'd grab any fix, even a bad one. A bad fix people pay for proves the pain.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: iD grew into a ₹100 crore company, but the same clue works in a colony. Imagine you want to start a food business from home. You have ₹40,000 saved and three ideas, and you can only try one.

screens.prompt: Which of your three ideas has the strongest proof that people need it?

options.label: Eggless cakes. Mothers take an auto 6 km to buy them
Fusion cakes. 40 friends at your party told you to start
Home cleaning. An app says demand is growing fast in your city

screens.why: Yes. The mothers already spend time and auto fare on a clumsy fix. That trouble, in your own colony, is your proof.

wrong.b: Telling you to start costs your friends nothing. Nobody is going to any trouble for fusion cakes yet.
wrong.c: Growth across a city tells you nothing about your street. Nobody near you is doing anything to get home cleaning yet.

screens.prompt: 30 families each buy 4 eggless cakes a year, with a ₹120 auto trip per cake. You deliver for ₹40. What do they save yearly?
screens.why: Right. 30 × 4 = 120 cakes. Each saves ₹120 − ₹40 = ₹80, and 120 × ₹80 = ₹9,600 a year. That's what your service is worth to them, in rupees.

wrong.a: That's what they spend on autos now: 120 trips × ₹120. But they'd still pay you ₹40 a cake, so each saves ₹80: 120 × ₹80 = ₹9,600.
wrong.c: That's 120 × ₹40, what they'd pay you for delivery. The saving is ₹120 − ₹40 = ₹80 a cake: 120 × ₹80 = ₹9,600.

screens.title: When nobody has a fix
screens.text: Sometimes nobody has a fix because none exists yet. That can still be a great problem, if people keep looking for one, again and again. But if there's no fix and nobody even looks, the pain is probably small. Check before you spend.

screens.prompt: Here are three problems in your colony. Which one is most worth checking first?

options.label: Late-night snacks. No shop opens after 11. Nobody minds
Tailoring. Two busy tailors nearby, and people are happy
Pet care. Owners keep posting "Who can feed my cat?"

screens.why: Yes. Nobody offers pet care, but owners keep looking for help. That's a real need, even with no fix around yet.

wrong.a: No shop, and nobody minds: that usually means small pain. Pet owners who keep posting for help show a much stronger need.
wrong.b: People already have a fix that works, and they're happy. The pet owners keep looking for help and find none.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six things you might notice. For each one, tell me: are people already going to trouble about it?

items.text: Parents pay a cousin ₹200 a week to fetch tiffin from a cook 3 km away
Friends say they'd love a gym in the colony
Shopkeepers write udhaar in a notebook, and still lose money on dues they forget
Office workers queue 20 minutes every morning at the only breakfast cart nearby
In a survey, most people say they'd try a new snack

screens.why: Paying a cousin, a notebook that still loses money, a 20-minute queue: these are clumsy fixes people already put up with. Likes, surveys and "I'd love it" cost nothing, so they prove nothing yet.

screens.setup: You pick eggless cakes. A bakery 6 km away charges ₹700 for a 1 kg cake. You'll charge ₹700 too, plus ₹40 to deliver, which pays for petrol. Each cake costs you ₹350 to make. You have ₹40,000 saved. A neighbour says, "A shop on the main road, at ₹15,000 a month, would bring walk-in buyers from the whole area."
screens.question: How do you start?

options.label: Rent the shop for walk-in buyers from the whole area
options.outcome: You rent the shop. In the first month you sell 20 cakes, which leaves you ₹7,000. The rent is ₹15,000, so you lose ₹8,000. At that rate, your ₹40,000 lasts five months.
options.why: The shop brought a few more sales, but not ₹15,000 more a month. The mothers' trouble was the 6 km trip, not a missing shop sign.
options.better: Bake at home and deliver to the colony mothers first.

options.label: Put up posters all over the area, then start
options.outcome: The posters cost ₹3,000. A few strangers call, but most orders still come from colony mothers who heard about you from each other.
options.why: Posters reach everyone, but your strongest buyers were already known: the mothers making the 6 km trip.
options.better: Start with the mothers who already take an auto 6 km for these cakes.

options.label: Bake at home and deliver in the colony first
options.outcome: Twelve mothers order in the first month. Each cake leaves you ₹350, so you keep ₹4,200, and you pay no rent. Your ₹40,000 is still safe.
options.why: You went straight to the people already going to trouble, and kept your costs tiny. That's where first orders come from.

screens.text: Words alone cost ___. A bad fix that people still ___ for proves the pain.
screens.why: Right. Likes and "I'd love it" cost nothing. iD's buyers kept paying for messy bags, and your colony mothers pay for autos. That's the proof.

summary: Workaround: a clumsy fix people use because nothing better exists.
If people already pay or go to trouble for a bad fix, the pain is real.
If nobody bothers with any fix, ask why before you spend.

cards.front: Which is better proof that people want home tiffin?
options: Families pay ₹200 a week to fetch tiffin from far away
cards.back: Paying ₹200 a week is a workaround. Likes cost nothing.

cards.front: Nobody in your area does anything about a problem. What should you ask first?
options: Does it hurt enough to bother?
cards.back: No fix and no complaints often means small pain. Check before you spend.

cards.front: 20 families each make 5 trips a year, at ₹100 a trip. What do they spend on trips?
